Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:46: "A humble spirit" is the attribute called "spirit," which is well known, and "humble" — for we find (Psalms 34:19), "the LORD is near to the brokenhearted, and He saves the crushed in spirit," and likewise (Isaiah 57:15), "I dwell in the high and holy place, and with the crushed and humble of spirit."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:47: "A lowly soul" is in the place of the soul, which is the place of lowliness — the poor and lowly ones who do not pursue desire, and here is the place of the poor and lowly, to whom was given the gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner [of the field] — all of whose amounts are small: two omers is a "forgotten sheaf" but three is not, two stalks is a "gleaning" but three is not, etc., as explained in the Mishnah (Pe'ah 6:5). And likewise Ruth, who corresponds to this attribute, said (Ruth 2:2), "let me go, please, and glean among the ears" — content with little and not pursuing desire; and so Boaz said to her (ibid. 3:10), "you have made your last kindness better than the first, in not going after the young men, whether poor or rich" — this too being the breaking of desire.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:48: Behold, these three encompass all the supernal attributes, and it is possible to say that this is what our Sages of blessed memory intended in the statement we copied at the beginning of the chapter — that from the Torah, from the Prophets, and from the Writings, we find everywhere that where the might of the Holy One, blessed be He, is stated, His humility is recognized there. And the reason this matter appears in Torah, Prophets, and Writings may be said to correspond to these three places mentioned, and there is likewise an allusion in the verses the author of the statement brought, as the reader will note upon examining them precisely.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:49: Rabbi Yosef Yavetz wrote that these three mentioned — good eye, etc. — correspond to Neshamah, Ruach, Nefesh: "good eye" corresponds to Neshamah, and therefore he loses the desire of this world, since he builds his levels in heaven. "Humble spirit" corresponds to Ruach — this is humility. "Lowly soul" corresponds to Nefesh. And he wrote: whoever is complete in these attributes, three gates of the Garden of Eden will be opened for him, for his flesh shall dwell securely in the grave and his soul shall be guarded, as it is written (Proverbs 6:22), "when you walk it shall guide you" etc., and as explained in the Zohar, that his ruach goes to the lower Garden of Eden and his neshamah to Eden [proper], and the head of the Garden of Eden is Abraham our father, peace be upon him — meaning, a father of holy souls, as the verse says (Malachi 2:10), "have we not all one father?" And whoever possesses the three attributes of the wicked Balaam, three gates of Gehinnom will be opened for him, for these three [good] attributes were emanated to Israel from the sefirah of purity, and [those] of the idolatrous nations of the world are the opposite. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 1:50: Now that we have explained the general attributes of humility in this chapter — which, as explained, encompass all the attributes — we shall come in the next chapter to explain the punishments for pride and its blemish, so that a person distance himself from pride and from anger, whether out of love or out of fear; and since it is better that a person do his deeds for the sake of Heaven, out of love, to resemble his Creator, we have therefore placed this preceding chapter first:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:1: Just as humility is one of the great virtues of the soul — so much so that to merit it a person must first attain several attributes we explained in the Gate of Love (ch. 11) regarding the statement of Rabbi Pinchas (Avodah Zarah 20b), "purity brings one to holiness," and according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, humility is greater than all of them — so too pride is an attribute that lowers the soul from the place of supernal holiness to the lowest level, as it is written (Proverbs 29:23), "a person's pride shall bring him low." And so our Sages of blessed memory said in tractate Avodah Zarah, chapter 1 (18b): Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, whoever is arrogant falls into Gehinnom, as it is said (Proverbs 21:24), "the proud, arrogant one, scoffer is his name, acting with the wrath of arrogance" — and "wrath" [evrah] is nothing but Gehinnom, as it is said (Zephaniah 1:15), "that day is a day of wrath." Thus far his words. And he used the term "falls" to show that it is like those who fall, falling from a high place to a low place, and there is nothing lower than Gehinnom — a sign for this: there is nothing higher than "Oneg" [delight] and nothing lower than "Nega" [affliction] (cf. Sefer Yetzirah 2:7) [same Hebrew letters rearranged].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:2: It is already known that our Sages of blessed memory explained (Tanchuma, Metzora 4) that tzara'at afflictions come for eleven things, and one of them is haughtiness of spirit. And in Tanchuma (there) they proved this from Na'aman, and in one place (Vayikra Rabbah 17:3) from what is written (2 Chronicles 26:16), "and when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:3: The reason for this is that a person was created from the beginning only so that he recognize the greatness of the Holy One, blessed be He, and serve Him like a servant who serves his master — for there is no pride for a servant before his master. Now, there is no [legitimate] pride except before the Master of all, to whom all are subjugated, as explained in the Gate of Awe, chapter 2. Nevertheless, all things emanated, created, and made acknowledge His providence and are subjugated to His word, knowing that all their life-force and flow come from Him, blessed be He. But one who is arrogant indicates that he has no master, thereby uprooting himself from the holy place to the place of impurity, which denies providence — for the serpent denied providence when it enticed Adam and his wife, saying (Genesis 3:5), "and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil," and our Sages of blessed memory said (Bereshit Rabbah 19:4) that the serpent said to her, "from this tree the Holy One, blessed be He, ate and created the world, and He is jealous" etc. — thus he indicated duality [in the Godhead] and denied the very principle of everything.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:4: Therefore our Sages of blessed memory commanded us (Avot 4:4), "be exceedingly, exceedingly humble of spirit" — for although in other good qualities the middle path is the best of qualities, regarding humility one must go to the very extreme, so as to distance himself entirely from pride, lest even a trace of the kelipah attach to him. Therefore they said in tractate Sotah (5a): Rav Nachman said, not even a small amount of it, nor any part of it — is it a small thing what is written of it (Proverbs 16:5), "an abomination to the LORD is every proud heart"? Thus far his words. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained that it calls it an abomination [to'evah]. And the explanation is that it is already known that "to'evah" refers to idolatry, as it is written (Deuteronomy 7:26), "and do not bring an abomination into your house." And likewise it says just before this (4b), regarding the punishments for pride and haughtiness of spirit: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, whoever has haughtiness of spirit is as though he worships idols — here it is written "an abomination to the LORD is every proud heart," and there it is written "do not bring an abomination into your house." And Rabbi Yochanan himself said, it is as though he denies the very foundation [of faith], as it is said (Deuteronomy 8:14), "and your heart becomes proud and you forget the LORD your God" etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:5: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina said, it is as though he has relations with all the forbidden unions — here it is written "an abomination to the LORD is every proud heart," and there it is written (Leviticus 18:27), "for the men of the land who were before you did all these abominations." Ulla said, it is as though he built a high place [bamah] for idolatry, as it is said (Isaiah 2:22), "cease for yourselves from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for wherein [bameh] is he to be accounted?" — do not read "bameh" but "bamah."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:6: From where do we know the warning against haughty-spirited people? Rava said in the name of Ze'iri (Jeremiah 13:15), "hear and give ear, do not be haughty." Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak [derives it] from here (Deuteronomy 8:14), "and your heart becomes proud and you forget the LORD your God," and it is written, "take heed lest you forget the LORD your God" (ibid. 6:12) — and in accordance with what Rabbi Avin said in the name of Rabbi Ela, that wherever it says "take heed," "lest," or "do not," it refers only to a negative commandment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:7: Rav Avira expounded — sometimes he said it in the name of Rabbi Asi, and sometimes in the name of Rabbi Ami — whoever has haughtiness of spirit is ultimately diminished, as it is said (Job 24:24), "they are exalted for a little while, then are gone." And should you say he still exists in the world — the verse teaches, "and are not." And if he repents, he is gathered from the world in his own time, like Abraham our father, as it is said, "and brought low, they are gathered like all others; they are cut off" — like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, of whom "all," "from all," and "all" are written. Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "they are exalted for a little while" — his importance diminishes; "gone" — he no longer exists; "and brought low" — but if he repents and becomes lowly, humble, lowering himself; "like all" — like those of whom "all" is said; "they are gathered" — from the world, dying the death of the upright. Of Abraham it is written (Genesis 24:1), "the LORD had blessed Abraham with all [ba'kol]"; of Isaac it is written (ibid. 27:33), "and I ate of all [mikol]"; of Jacob it is written (ibid. 33:11), "for God has been gracious to me and I have all [kol]" — and this is explicitly explained in Bereshit Rabbah. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:8: Further there, the completion of this statement: and if not (Job 24:24), "they wither like the top of an ear of grain." What is "like the top of an ear of grain"? Rav Huna and Rav Chisda — one said, like the beard/awn of the ear, and one said, like the ear itself. According to the one who said "like the beard of the ear," this matches "the top of the ear," but according to the one who said "like the ear itself," why "the top of the ear"? Rav Asi said, and so it was taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael: a parable of a man who enters his field — whichever [ears] are tallest, he gathers. Thus far his words. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: the "beard" of the ear is the tall part of the grain-ear, called the "beard of the ear," which breaks and falls by itself. "Whichever is tallest he gathers" — this is "they wither like the top of an ear of grain" — like the ear whose head appears above its fellows.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:9: Further there, Rabbi Elazar said, whoever has haughtiness of spirit deserves to be cut down like an asherah [idolatrous tree] — here it is written (Isaiah 10:33), "and the lofty of stature shall be cut down," and there it is written (Deuteronomy 7:5), "and their asherim you shall cut down." And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "like an asherah" — he shall be cut down and his roots pursued after, like an asherah which must be uprooted down to its roots, as it is written (Deuteronomy 12:3), "and you shall destroy their name."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:10: Further there, Rabbi Elazar said, whoever has haughtiness of spirit — his dust will not be stirred [in resurrection], as it is said (Isaiah 26:19), "awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust" — it does not say "you who lie in the dust" but "you who dwell in the dust" — one who became a neighbor to dust in his lifetime. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "stirred" — awakened in the resurrection of the dead; it does not say "those who lie in the dust," which would apply to all the dead; "a neighbor to dust" — one who lowers himself down to the dust [in life, i.e., only he shall be raised].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:11: And Rabbi Elazar said, whoever has haughtiness of spirit, the Shechinah wails over him, as it is said (Psalms 138:6), "and the lofty He knows from afar." And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "wails" — laments; "and the lofty He knows from afar" — the beginning of the verse is "for the LORD is high, yet He sees the lowly, and the lofty He knows from afar" — even before the retribution comes upon him, many days in advance, "He knows" — the Shechinah mourns and grieves over him, as in (Judges 8:16), "and he made known [vayoda] with them the men of Sukkot," and "and made known her widowhood" [others: "chastened her widows," a play on similar roots] (Ezekiel 19:7), "He has made known [hodia] as though bringing above" (Psalms 74:5) — a term of breaking.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:12: Rav Avira expounded, and some say it was Rabbi Elazar: come and see, the attribute of the Holy One, blessed be He, is not like the attribute of flesh and blood — the attribute of flesh and blood is that the high sees the high but the high does not see the low; but the attribute of the Holy One, blessed be He, is not so: He is high, yet sees the low, as it is said, "for the LORD is high, yet He sees the lowly." And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "He sees the lowly" — to draw him near and take pains with him and consider him precious in His eyes, as in (Hosea 9:10), "like the first fruit on the fig tree in its beginning, I saw your fathers" — I set My eyes upon them to draw them near and cherish them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:13: Rav Chisda said, and some say Mar Ukva: whoever has haughtiness of spirit — the Holy One, blessed be He, says, "he and I cannot dwell in the world," as it is said (Psalms 101:5), "whoever slanders his fellow in secret, him I will destroy; the haughty-eyed and proud of heart, him [oto] I cannot [endure]" — do not read "oto" but "ito" [with him, I cannot dwell]. Some teach it regarding those who speak evil speech, as it is said, "whoever slanders his fellow in secret, him I will destroy." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:14: Further there, Chizkiyah said, a person's prayer is not heard unless he makes his heart like flesh, as it is said (Isaiah 66:23), "and it shall be that from new moon to new moon... all flesh shall come [to worship before Me]." Rabbi Zeira said, of "flesh" it is written "and he shall be healed," but of "man" it is not written "and he shall be healed." And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "like flesh," which is soft, and not like stone, which is hard. "To worship" — to pray; those who are like flesh will come and pray, for they are heard before Me, but the haughty-spirited will not come. "Of flesh it is written 'and he shall be healed'" — as in "or if there be in the skin of his flesh a boil, and it is healed" (Leviticus 13:18); "if a man have in the skin of his flesh" (ibid. 13:2); "if the plague of tzara'at be in a man" (ibid. 13:9) — in none of these is "and he shall be healed" written; from your own reasoning you learn that whoever is soft and humble, like flesh, is close to being healed from the sufferings that come upon him, but whoever is hard like the earth, there is no healing for his wounds.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:15: Rabbi Yochanan said, "ADaM" [man] — *ashes, *blood, *bile [mar'ah]; "BaSaR" [flesh] — *shame [bushah], *stench [sirachon], *worm [rimah]. Some say: *shame, *the grave [she'ol], *worm — since it is spelled with a shin [in some readings]. Thus far his words. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "adam" — why is he called Adam? Because he is ashes, blood, and bile — meaning, he is entirely vanity, and therefore should not be proud. "Bile" [marah] is the bitter fluid that comes from the gallbladder in the liver and is strengthened in a person according to the seasons, the changing of times, and the food he eats, and through it come illnesses, afflictions, and pains — some doctors call it black bile, some call it red bile. "She'ol" [the grave] — the place from which he is asked [she'ul, related to she'ol] for his house [i.e., death demands it], etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:16: Further there, Rav Ashi said, whoever has haughtiness of spirit is ultimately diminished, as it is said (Leviticus 14:56), "and for a rising [se'et], and for a scab [sapachat], and for a bright spot" — and "se'et" means nothing but high, as it is said (Isaiah 2:13), "and upon all the high mountains, and upon all the raised hills" — and "sapachat" [scab, related to "attach/diminish"] means nothing but subordinate, as it is said (1 Samuel 2:36), "attach me [safcheni], please" etc. Thus far his words. Here end the punishments mentioned there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:17: When a person takes to heart all the punishments mentioned, the greatest of which is that he has no resurrection at the time of the resurrection of the dead, he will lower the height of his pride, and consider that it would have been better for him not to have been created — for the proper fate of a person is that he live in the resurrection of the dead, as explained in the Gate of Love (ch. 6), and one who is proud attaches himself so much to the kelipah that his very body is nearly deprived of coming to life.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:18: Besides all the punishments mentioned, when a person takes to heart what is mentioned at the end of the statements cited in Rabbi Yochanan's saying — that man is "BaSaR": shame, stench, worm, or shame, the grave, worm — the meaning is that there is no shame like the shame of sins, when they are shown to him before all the retinue of Heaven, and upon seeing his evil deeds, will he not then be ashamed and disgraced, with no mouth to answer and no forehead to raise his head, as the prophet said (Jeremiah 3:25), "let us lie down in our shame, and let our disgrace cover us, for we have sinned against the LORD our God"?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:19: "Stench" comes from his being drawn after the desires of the world, and thereby he becomes rank; therefore it is fitting to distance oneself from worldly acquisitions and the pursuit of luxuries, whose end is stench, and it is luxuries that bring one to haughtiness of heart.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:20: Or when he considers that the grave is the place of his house, why then should he be in the world, and why should he be proud? Is he not placed in the lowliest of places, and if his sins should cause him to descend to Gehinnom, all the more so is it fitting for him to mourn and humble himself over his sins and lower the height of his pride, since this is his end if he does not repent.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:21: "Worm" refers to the judgment of the grave, as explained in the Gate of Awe — and when a person wishes to be proud of his beauty, his garments, or his wealth, let him consider that in the end all of it will be eaten by the worm; he should not be proud of anything of the world's affairs, for all its goodness comes to an end and ceases, being entirely clothed in the filth of the serpent that brought death into the world. A person has nothing from this world except the commandments and the Torah, which are spiritual, and cling to the enduring spiritual soul, which cleaves to its Maker after its judgment is completed and it is appeased upon the altar through Michael, the great prince, as explained in the Zohar (portion Metzora, 53b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:22: Likewise, among the things that bring about humility and lowliness is when a person considers the greatness of our Creator, the Creator of all, King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, whose greatness has no limit and no end, as we have elaborated in the Gate of Awe. This brings about humility, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 8:4), "when I see Your heavens, the work of Your fingers" etc., "what is man that You are mindful of him?" — for even the whole world under the dome of the firmament is like a mustard seed; if so, the people of the world within it are considered as nothing, as it is said (Daniel 4:32), "and all the inhabitants of the earth are considered as nothing."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:23: And if he becomes proud of his wisdom, let him think of the wisdom of the ancient sages, and then he will see that all our wisdom is considered like the peel of garlic before their wisdom. Moreover, according to one's wisdom must be one's awe and deeds, for "an unwitting error in study is counted as deliberate" (Avot 4:13), as we have elaborated in the Gate of Awe (ch. 4), as our Sages of blessed memory said in Bereshit Rabbah (19:1) regarding "and the serpent was cunning" (Genesis 3:1), that they said, according to his wisdom was his downfall — "cunning" from "cursed" [ha-arum from arur] — and similarly (Ecclesiastes 1:18), "and he who increases knowledge increases sorrow," for a stain that falls on a silk garment is not the same as a stain that falls on a linen garment, since according to its costliness it will be hard to remove.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:24: And if he becomes proud of his wealth, he must fear lest that wealth turn to his detriment, or lest he not fulfill his obligation in what his Creator has graciously given him to give to the poor.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:25: Likewise, among the things that bring a person to a humbled heart is when he considers what we explained in the Gate of Awe, in several aspects, that sin darkens the soul, blemishes the supernal worlds, and causes the exile of the Shechinah — and then he will think in his soul and say in his heart that it would have been better for him not to have been created, since he causes such great evil.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:26: Therefore it is fitting for a person to flee from pride and dominion, for pride is the root of all bad qualities and brings a person to several sins, as explained in the Zohar (portion Vayikra, 23a) on the verse (Leviticus 4:22), "when [asher] a ruler sins" — these are his words: Rabbi Yitzchak taught, why does it differ, that everywhere else it is written "and if" [ve'im], as in (ibid. 4:3), "if the anointed priest sins," and "and if the whole congregation of Israel errs" (ibid. 4:13), but here "when a ruler sins," not "and if a ruler sins"? What is the meaning of this? Rather, these priests are not usually found sinning in this way, for they always guard themselves since their Master's burden is upon them every day, and the burden of all Israel, and the burden of each and every one; therefore it is astonishing when he sins, and therefore "and if" is written. Likewise "and if the whole congregation of Israel errs" — it is astonishing that they are all found in a single sin, for if these sin, those do not sin — therefore "and if" is written. But "when a ruler sins" is certain, since his heart is proud within him, and the people follow after him and are appointed under him; therefore "when a ruler sins," such as transgressing a negative commandment, and he does one of them — therefore "and if" is not written of him, for his words are not in doubt. Thus far his words. And likewise, just before this in the same portion, end of 8: he says, and all sins are found only among the wealthy, since their hearts are proud within them, and are not found among the poor. Therefore it is fitting for a person to distance himself from leadership and dominion, so that his heart not become proud and he sin.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:27: Honor is one of the things that remove one from this world and the World to Come. From this world, our Sages of blessed memory said in tractate Berachot (55a) that three things shorten a person's days, and one of them is one who conducts himself with leadership — for Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina said, why did Joseph die before his brothers? Because he conducted himself with leadership over them. Thus far his words. And this statement is likewise found in Sotah (13b). Rabbi Yochanan said, woe to leadership, which buries its holders (Pesachim 87b).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:28: Further, our Sages of blessed memory elaborated at length in the Pesikta (Rabbati, ch. 22) on the verse (Proverbs 6:32), "whoever commits adultery lacks sense," how much one must distance oneself. These are his words: Rabbi Menachma in the name of Rabbi Tanchum bar Chiya, Rabbi Mani in the name of Rabbi Yosi ben Zevida: "whoever commits adultery lacks sense" — whoever accepts leadership upon himself in order to benefit from it is nothing but like this adulterer, who benefits from a woman's body. "He destroys his own soul who does this" — like Moses, who said (Exodus 32:32), "and now, if You will forgive their sin — and if not, blot me, please" [from Your book]; like Joshua, who said (Joshua 7:8), "O LORD" [taking responsibility] — "me, and not them"; like David, who said (1 Chronicles 21:17), "let Your hand, please, be against me and against my father's house, but not against Your people, to be a plague."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:29: Rabbi Menachma bar Yaakov brings it from here (Proverbs 25:8), "do not go out to strive hastily" — this is written for a judge: never run after leadership, why? "Lest — what will you do in the end, when your fellow puts you to shame?" — tomorrow they come and ask you questions, what will you answer? Rabbi Ze'ira brings it from here: "you shall not carry [lo tissa]" (Exodus 20:7) — if the verse speaks of a false oath, it has already said (Leviticus 19:12), "and you shall not swear falsely by My Name" — so what does "you shall not carry" teach? That you should not take upon yourself leadership if you are not fit for leadership. Rabbi Abahu said, [God says] I am called holy and you are called holy — if you do not have all the qualities that I have, do not accept leadership upon yourself.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:30: "Whoever commits adultery lacks sense" — the Holy One, blessed be He, removes wisdom from his heart, and "wisdom" is nothing but Torah, as it is said (Psalms 19:8), "making the simple wise," and moreover, his radiant countenance changes; and when the Day of Judgment comes, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not forgive him but is filled with wrath against him, as it is said (Proverbs 6:34), "he will not spare on the day of vengeance." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:31: Further, regarding his punishment in the World to Come, they said in tractate Rosh Hashanah, chapter 1 (17a): but the Sadducees, the informers, and the heretics who denied the Torah, denied the resurrection of the dead, separated from the ways of the community, and cast their terror in the land of the living, etc., descend to Gehinnom and are judged there for generations upon generations, as it is said (Isaiah 66:24), "and they shall go out and look upon the corpses of the men who rebelled against Me" etc. — Gehinnom is consumed but they are not consumed, as it is said (Psalms 49:15), "and their form shall wear away, the grave" etc. And we say further there, regarding "cast their terror in the land of the living": Rav Chisda said, this refers to a communal leader who casts excessive terror upon the community not for the sake of Heaven. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav, any communal leader who casts excessive terror upon the community not for the sake of Heaven will not see a Torah-scholar son of his own, as it is said (Job 37:24), "therefore men fear Him; he does not regard any who are wise of heart." Thus far his words. We find, then, that the punishment for one who pursues leadership has punishment in this world and immeasurable punishment in the World to Come, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:32: Haughtiness of spirit removed Jeroboam ben Nevat from the World to Come, and so they said in Sanhedrin (101b): Rav Nachman said, the haughtiness of spirit that was in Jeroboam drove him from the World to Come, as it is said (1 Kings 12:26), "and Jeroboam said in his heart, now the kingdom will return to the house of David if this people go up to offer sacrifices in the house of the LORD... and they will return" etc. "to Rechavam, king of Judah." He said, it is a tradition that sitting in the Temple courtyard is only for kings of the house of David; when they see him sitting while I stand, they will say, this one is king and that one is not king, and they will kill me and go to him. Immediately (ibid. 12:28), "and the king took counsel and made two golden calves," and said to them, it is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem. Thus far his words, as relevant to our purpose.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:33: Moreover, even a Torah scholar, if he becomes proud of his wisdom, his wisdom departs and he forgets his learning, as we say in Pesachim (66b): Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav, whoever is arrogant — if he is a prophet, his prophecy departs from him; if he is a sage, his wisdom departs. That his wisdom departs if he is a sage, from where do we learn this? From Hillel — for the master said, he began to provoke them with words and said to them, what caused you that I should come up from Babylonia and become your leader? The laziness that was in you, that you did not serve the two greatest men of the generation, Shemayah and Avtalyon — and he said to them, this halakhah I heard and forgot. That his prophecy departs if he is a prophet, from where do we learn this? From Deborah, as it is said (Judges 5:7), "the villages ceased" etc. "until I, Deborah, arose" etc., and it is written (ibid. 5:12), "awake, awake, Deborah" [implying she needed to be re-aroused since prophecy had departed]. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:34: Likewise they said in the Midrash on the verse (Job 9:7), "who commands the sun and it does not rise": our Sages of blessed memory said (Yalkut, Job §904): and so you find with the greatest of the prophets — because he said (Deuteronomy 1:17), "and the matter that is too difficult for you" [bring to me], the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, by your life, even a matter that women know you do not know, as it is said (Numbers 27:5), "and Moses brought their case before the LORD," and it is written (ibid. 27:7), "the daughters of Zelophehad speak correctly." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:35: Further, we say in Kiddushin (49b), regarding what is said, ten measures of haughtiness of spirit descended to the world, nine were taken by Elam and one by the whole rest of the world — and it raises a difficulty: but did no haughtiness of spirit descend to Babylonia? etc. — and it further raises a difficulty: but did not the master say, the sign of haughtiness of spirit is poverty, and Babylonia has poverty? What poverty? Poverty of Torah, as it is written (Song of Songs 8:8), "we have a little sister" — Rabbi Yochanan said, this is Elam, which merited to learn but did not merit to teach. Thus far his words.
